title: HTTP Caching
summary: This document defines HTTP caches and the header fields that control cache behavior or mark responses as cacheable. It is part of the revised HTTP specification and obsoletes RFC 7234.

plainLanguage.summary: HTTP caches keep response copies so they can answer later requests without always contacting the origin server. RFC 9111 defines when those copies can be kept, reused, checked, or discarded.

questions: what is the difference between no-cache and no-store
how does http cache validation work
subtitle: The rules for storing HTTP responses, deciding when they are fresh, and checking them with the origin server.

tldr.problem: Fetching the same response repeatedly uses time and network capacity, while reusing an unsuitable stored response can return outdated or private information.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9111 defines cache storage, cache keys, freshness, validation, invalidation, and directives such as Cache-Control, Age, and Expires.
tldr.outcome: It is Internet Standard STD 98 and obsoletes RFC 7234. It deprecates Pragma and obsoletes Warning.

today: RFC 9111 is Internet Standard STD 98 and obsoletes RFC 7234.

sections.title: What an HTTP Cache Does
sections.content:
An HTTP cache is a local store of response messages and the subsystem that controls their storage, retrieval, and deletion. Reusing a stored response can reduce response time and network bandwidth. Caching is optional in HTTP, and a cache may be private to one user or shared among several users.

A cache uses a cache key to select a stored response. At minimum, the key includes the request method and target URI. The Vary response field can make request header values part of the key when a resource returns different representations for different requests.
sections.plainLanguage: A cache saves HTTP responses so it can answer some later requests from a stored copy. It must select a copy that matches the request.

sections.title: Storing and Reusing Responses
sections.content:
A cache must not store a response unless it understands the request method, the response is final, and the response is eligible for caching. For example, no-store prevents storage, and a shared cache must respect private and rules for requests containing Authorization. Cache extensions can change some of these requirements.

Before reuse, the cache checks the target URI and method, request fields named by Vary, and whether the response is fresh, permitted to be served stale, or successfully validated. When it reuses a response without validation, it generates an Age field. Unsafe requests must be forwarded to the origin server before the cache replies.
sections.plainLanguage: Before saving a response, the cache checks whether the rules allow it. Before reusing one, it checks that it matches the request and is fresh or has been validated.

sections.title: Freshness and Response Age
sections.content:
A response is fresh while its age is less than its freshness lifetime; otherwise it is stale. A cache uses the first available source of freshness information: s-maxage for shared caches, then max-age, then the difference between Expires and Date. If no explicit expiration exists, a cache may use a heuristic only when the response is eligible for heuristic freshness.

A response's age estimates the time since it was generated or successfully validated at the origin. A cache must not serve stale data when an applicable directive forbids it. Without a clock, a cache must revalidate stored responses every time it uses them.
sections.plainLanguage: A response can be reused without checking the origin while it remains fresh. After it becomes stale, the cache follows the response's rules about checking or serving it.

sections.title: Validation and Invalidation
sections.content:
When a stored response cannot be reused as it is, a cache can send a conditional request with validators from the stored response. These may include an entity tag in If-None-Match or a modification time in If-Modified-Since. A 304 Not Modified response lets the cache update the stored response and reuse it; a full response replaces it.

When an unsafe request such as PUT, POST, or DELETE receives a successful or redirection response, a cache must invalidate the target URI. It may invalidate related URIs from Location or Content-Location, but not when their origin differs from the target URI's origin.
sections.plainLanguage: A cache can ask the origin whether its stored response is still valid. A successful change request also makes the cache remove or recheck the response for the changed address.

sections.title: Cache-Control Directives and Security
sections.content:
Cache-Control carries directives for caches along a request and response chain. Response directives must be followed. For example, max-age sets a freshness period, no-cache requires validation before reuse, no-store prohibits storage, and private prevents a shared cache from storing the response. s-maxage sets the freshness period for shared caches.

Cache contents can reveal information and can be poisoned with malicious responses. A cache can also reveal which resources were requested through timing differences. The RFC warns that Set-Cookie does not itself prevent caching; servers should use suitable Cache-Control fields for responses they need to control.
sections.plainLanguage: Cache-Control tells caches how long they may keep a response and when they must check it again. Stored responses can reveal user activity, so caches and their contents need protection.
